title: Distributed Job Scheduler
prompt:
Design a platform that lets teams schedule jobs to run at specific times or on cron schedules (like a distributed cron / Airflow-lite).

Functional requirements:
- Register jobs with a cron expression or a one-time run time, a payload (container image or HTTP callback), timeout, and retry policy.
- Jobs run at their scheduled time within a few seconds of accuracy.
- A scheduled run should execute once; retries on failure per policy.
- Users can view run history, pause, and trigger jobs manually.
- Optional dependencies: job B runs after job A succeeds.

Scale:
- 10M registered jobs; up to 50k job runs starting in the same minute at peak (e.g. top of the hour).
- Job durations from seconds to hours.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you find jobs that are due without scanning all 10M every second?
2. How do you avoid double execution when scheduler nodes fail or network partitions occur?
3. How do workers pick up, heartbeat, and report on runs?
4. How do you handle the top-of-the-hour thundering herd?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 50k runs in a minute = ~830/s spikes, much higher if all at second zero.
- Run history: assume 100M runs/day x 500 bytes = 50 GB/day.

DATA MODEL
- jobs(job_id, owner, schedule, payload, timeout, retry_policy, paused, next_run_at).
- runs(run_id, job_id, scheduled_time, attempt, status, worker_id, lease_expires_at, started_at, finished_at). Unique (job_id, scheduled_time) prevents duplicate run creation.

FINDING DUE JOBS
- Index on next_run_at. Partition jobs into N buckets (hash of job_id); each scheduler node owns a set of buckets (lease via etcd/ZooKeeper).
- Each scheduler polls its buckets every second for next_run_at <= now + lookahead, creates run rows, and enqueues them; then computes and stores the next next_run_at. Alternative: a hierarchical timing wheel in memory loaded with the next few minutes of jobs.

EXACTLY-ONCE (EFFECTIVELY)
- Run creation is idempotent via the unique (job_id, scheduled_time) constraint, so two schedulers racing for the same bucket after a failover cannot create duplicate runs.
- Execution is at-least-once: workers claim runs with a lease (conditional update status QUEUED -> RUNNING with lease_expires_at, owner). Workers heartbeat to extend the lease. If a lease expires, the run is re-queued.
- Pass a fencing token (attempt number) to the job so downstream systems can reject stale attempts. Job authors must still make handlers idempotent; true exactly-once side effects are not achievable in general.

WORKERS
- Pull model from a queue (Kafka/SQS) partitioned by priority/tenant; workers launch containers or call HTTP callbacks with timeout enforcement.
- Results written back to runs; retries scheduled with backoff by creating a new attempt with a future time.

THUNDERING HERD
- Pre-enqueue with lookahead so runs are ready to dispatch at the exact second.
- Allow jobs to declare a jitter window; spread non-critical jobs automatically.
- Per-tenant concurrency quotas so one team cannot starve others.
- Autoscale worker pools ahead of known peaks.

DEPENDENCIES
- DAG stored per workflow; on run success, a coordinator marks downstream nodes ready when all parents succeeded.

PITFALLS
- Single leader scheduler with no failover, or failover without fencing.
- Using local cron on many machines.
- Missed runs after downtime: define a catch-up policy (run once, run all, skip).
- Time zones and DST for cron expressions.
